title: The coiled one remains
hook: what if four children were killed; the coiled serpent still lives, he writes (Zafarnama)

segments.voice: Yesterday, broken oaths: an emperor held to the promises he made in God's name. Your line was keep your oath. Did the promise you found get kept? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-three.

Some sentences are short because nothing more could be said. The Zafarnama has one of those. Sikh tradition remembers what came before the letter: the Guru's four sons were killed. Two, tradition says, fell fighting. Two, still small boys, were put to death because they would not give up their faith. A father who had lost all four children sat down and wrote to the emperor. The line he wrote about it is not a lament. It's a question, followed by an image Sikhs still repeat.
screen: `A SHORT SENTENCE.` → `FOUR SONS LOST.` → `A QUESTION, THEN AN IMAGE.`

segments.voice: Paraphrased, the line runs like this: what of it, if you have killed four children? The coiled serpent still remains. Hear how it's built. The first half names the worst thing that could happen to a parent, and names it flatly, almost as a shrug. That flatness is not coldness. It's refusal. He will not let the loss be the end of the sentence. The second half turns to the coiled one. A coiled snake is a snake at rest and fully alive, gathered into itself, not beaten. Readers hear different things in it. Some hear the Guru speaking of himself: you took my sons, and I am still here. Some hear the Khalsa, the community he had formed: you can kill children, and you have not killed the people. Some hear both, and a warning folded inside: a coiled thing can still rise. Whichever reading, the line is about what remains after the loss, not about the loss itself. And it's worth staying with what it doesn't say. It doesn't say the grief is small. Sikhs remember the four sons, the Sahibzade, with deep sorrow, in the Ardas and at gatherings that mark their deaths. The coiled one remains is not a way of skipping the mourning. It's what stands up in the middle of it.
screen: `WHAT OF IT, IF YOU KILLED FOUR CHILDREN?` · `A COILED SERPENT: AT REST, ALIVE.` · `THE GURU, THE KHALSA, OR BOTH?` · `NOT SKIPPING THE MOURNING.` · then, large: `STILL STANDING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand firm after a loss. Settle, and breathe. If it feels right, bring to mind a loss you've carried. It doesn't have to be the biggest one. A job, a friendship, a plan, a person. Let it be as heavy as it is; don't argue it down. Then, gently, look for what is still standing in you. A habit you kept. Someone you still look after. A way you still laugh. Rest your attention there, coiled and quiet, for a few breaths. If you pray, you can hold both the loss and what remains in Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
The coiled one remains. In the Zafarnama, after naming the killing of his four sons, Guru Gobind Singh writes that the coiled serpent still lives. Today's word.
Your line: still standing. Today, do one ordinary thing on purpose that the loss didn't take from you, and notice that you did it. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember the four Sahibzade in the Ardas and at gatherings that mark their martyrdom; the Zafarnama's line about the coiled serpent is often recited in katha and at those gatherings.

fork.setup: you've lost all four of your children, and you're writing to the man whose rule took them. what does your sentence about them do?
options: dwell on the grief for pages.
name the loss flatly, then say what remains.
fork.reveal: the Guru names it in a single question, what of it, if you killed four children? then turns at once: the coiled serpent still remains.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strange line about a snake.
what it means: you killed four children, and still the coiled one remains. the loss does not end the sentence.
what a scholar hears: readers take the coiled one as the Guru, the Khalsa, or both, and some hear a warning: a coiled thing can rise.

sources.ref: Zafarnama (Dasam Granth), the verse on the four children and the coiled serpent

notes: Both Zafarnama verses are paraphrased; please check the paraphrase ('what of it, if you have killed four children? the coiled serpent still remains') and that the sparks/fire image sits nearby.
The deaths of the four Sahibzade (two in battle, two put to death as small boys for refusing to give up their faith) are given as tradition; names, places and ages are deliberately left out.
The three readings of the coiled serpent (the Guru, the Khalsa, both) are offered as what readers hear; please confirm they are fair.
'Gather each winter to mark their deaths' refers to the Shaheedi commemorations in December (Poh); please confirm the wording.
Original left null: unsure of the exact Persian or Gurmukhi spelling of the 'coiled serpent' phrase.
